operationalization: A test would need a measure of how far selection is treated as a sufficient explanation and a measure of effort spent on physical causes of form, plus a result showing that the first suppresses the second. The claim does not fix either variable or a confirming threshold.
obstacles: The claim is about the effect of accepting an explanation, not about a biological measurement.
Publication counts cannot show that inquiry was stayed rather than redirected.
rationale: This is a claim about the philosophy of biological explanation. Bibliometric proxies for research effort exist, but they do not contain the causal notion of a satisfactory hypothesis holding inquiry back, and any historical pattern is compatible with several stories about why morphologists chose the problems they did. The claim therefore has no measurable consequence that separates it from its rivals.

operationalization: No particular variable, law, or mismatch is named. Any measured shape can be read as obeying physics, and also as physics plus an unmeasured non-physical contribution, so there is no result that would confirm or refute the claim as stated.
obstacles: The laws and the decision threshold are unspecified.
Unexplained form can always be assigned either to unknown physics or to a vital residue.
rationale: The statement is a universal programme for morphology rather than a relation between measured quantities. Morphometric archives contain shapes, not a variable called obedience to physical law. Because every finite set of forms is compatible both with the claim and with a rival that adds a non-physical cause, existing data do not discriminate it.

operationalization: Classifying the problems of form as mathematical and the problems of growth as physical is a statement about the kind of science morphology is. No observation would confirm or refute that classification.
obstacles: Disciplinary classification has no distinct empirical outcome.
rationale: The claim defines how morphological problems ought to be conceived. It does not assert a measurable relation among organisms, growth rates, or forms, so no dataset is relevant and no analysis could decide it.

operationalization: For named classes of law, compare measured osmotic equilibria, surface stresses, and chemical stoichiometry in cells and tissues with the values ordinary physics requires. A systematic, replicated violation would refute the claim for that law; agreement in a studied system would support only that restricted case.

candidate_datasets.name: BioNumbers
candidate_datasets.role: Literature-sourced cell concentrations, sizes, and physical constants used to check osmotic and surface quantities against ordinary physical ranges

obstacles: The claim is an open-ended negative over every law and every organism.
Agreement in model cells does not rule out a subtle non-physical contribution elsewhere.
rationale: Chemistry, surface action, and osmosis are specific enough that a quantitative violation in a well-measured system would count against the claim, and tabulated biophysical numbers exist for those checks. The scope is still all bodily mechanisms of all organisms, the phrase about what is known tracks the literature rather than a dataset, and consistency is weak evidence against a rival that allows rare exceptions. A small team could audit a few laws, not the universal claim.

operationalization: Where material properties and loads are known, compare an observed bone, shell, or cell outline with the shape predicted by force balance. A systematic mismatch would count against reading that outline as a diagram of those forces; agreement would support the reading only for that structure.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D meshes of bones, shells, and other hard parts on which a mechanical model can be compared with observed form

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Images of cell outlines for comparison with shapes expected from boundary forces

obstacles: Many different force histories fit one preserved shape.
Scans rarely include the material properties and boundary loads the deduction requires.
rationale: For a restricted class of structures the inverse mechanical problem is a standard analysis, and public 3D and image archives supply the shapes. The claim as stated covers any portion of matter, living or dead, and shape alone does not separate force balance from a growth programme that yields the same outline. That keeps the test partial and confounded outside well-posed cases such as loaded bone or a pressurized cell.

operationalization: Treat cortical tension as the modern stand-in for Thompson's interfacial tension, then relate measured boundary stress in amoeboid cells to outline curvature. The claim is favored if lowering that stress produces the protrusions and loss of rounding it requires, and weakened if shape is indifferent to boundary stress.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Public cell-imaging studies with outlines of amoeboid and other cells; tension itself is usually not in the archive

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Cell-shape images, including free-living amoebae, for morphometry of the fluid outline

obstacles: Cortical tension is an active regulated stress, not the passive surface tension of a fluid interface.
Paired tension-and-shape series sit in paper supplements rather than in the image archives.
rationale: The form of an amoeboid cell and its response to boundary stress are measurable, and a perturbation result would discriminate indifference to surface force from a strong effect. The mapping from classical surface tension to cortical tension is standard but not identical, which lowers operationalizability, and the tension values needed for the test have to be compiled. Image repositories cover shape for a useful but narrow set of cells.

operationalization: Compare cytoplasmic viscosity and creep of Amoeba, or closely similar naked cells, with water under small stress, and compare the flow timescale with the timescale of shape change. The claim is confirmed by ready flow, viscosity orders of magnitude above water, and a slowing of shape change by that viscosity; it is refuted if the material is elastic on that timescale or near water in viscosity.

candidate_datasets.name: BioNumbers
candidate_datasets.role: Published cytoplasmic viscosity and related physical constants for comparing cytoplasm with water

obstacles: Viscosities differ by method and are not gathered in one downloadable rheology table.
Active cytoskeletal flow can imitate high passive viscosity.
rationale: Viscosity, yield under slight pressure, and the timescale of shape change are standard variables, so the contrast with water and with an elastic solid is a real decision criterion. The measurements exist but are scattered across microrheology papers, cover a modest set of naked cells, and do not by themselves separate passive treacle-like viscosity from active flow. Compilation and that confound make the test partial rather than immediate.

operationalization: The claim asserts that there is no clear rule dividing vital from physical properties. A survey of how biologists classify phenomena would describe usage, not confirm or refute the absence of a rule.
obstacles: Denying a classification does not specify a distinguishing measurement.
rationale: This is a conceptual claim about categories. No dataset of organismal properties can show that a clear vital-versus-physical rule is impossible, because any proposed rule can be rejected as unclear without a measurable consequence that separates the claim from a rival rule.

operationalization: The wording says hereditary material never acts as matter alone but only as a seat of energy and a centre of force. Molecular and embryological measurements can be redescribed in those words, so they do not yield a distinct confirming or refuting result.
obstacles: The contrast between matter acting alone and matter as a centre of force is not an empirical contrast.
Sequence-specific effects in development are compatible with the claim under a change of vocabulary.
rationale: Applied to the nucleus, chromosomes, and germ-plasm, the sentence is a general thesis about dynamics rather than a prediction about inheritance. Existing developmental and genomic data describe material causes in detail, but both the claim and its rivals survive that description. It is not resolvable by analysis of those data.

operationalization: Compute k = W/L^3 for individual fish across lengths. A statistically flat k through the growing range would show stable general form at constant density; a systematic trend of k with length would show that form or density is changing while growth continues.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Species-level length-weight relationships from which the exponent and condition factor can be compared with the cube law

candidate_datasets.name: ICES DATRAS
candidate_datasets.role: Individual length and weight from trawl surveys, used to track k against length within species

obstacles: k mixes shape change with density, gut fullness, and gonad state.
Coverage is far stronger for commercial fishes than for growing animals in general.
rationale: The decision variable is the ordinary condition factor, and both a global compilation of length-weight fits and individual survey records are openly downloadable. A small team can test whether k stays constant during growth for many fishes in days. Density and reproductive state confound the step from a changing k to a change of form, and non-fish animals are thinly covered, but the relation as Thompson defined it for fishes is directly testable.

operationalization: Regress log stem diameter on log height. An exponent near 3/2 would support elastic similarity; exponents near 1 or 2 would favor geometric similarity or constant-stress scaling instead. The separate numerical cap of about 300 ft is checked by inserting the measured taper, density, and modulus of a pine of the Kew-flagstaff form into Greenhill's buckling formula.

candidate_datasets.name: Tallo
candidate_datasets.role: Individual tree stem diameter and height for fitting the diameter-height exponent across thousands of species

candidate_datasets.name: FIA DataMart
candidate_datasets.role: National forest inventory stem diameters and heights, including small stems, for the same allometric test

candidate_datasets.name: Global Wood Density Database
candidate_datasets.role: Wood density for thousands of taxa, one material constant in the self-buckling height calculation

obstacles: Inventories are cross-sectional, so young-versus-old slenderness is inferred from size rather than from followed stems.
Wind and hydraulics predict exponents similar to elastic buckling, and elastic modulus is not in the density table.
rationale: Diameter and height for hundreds of thousands of trees are already in open allometric tables, and a log-log comparison with the rival exponents 1 and 2 is a standard regression. That decides the scaling law that is the core of the claim, including the relative slenderness of smaller stems. The single-pine height of about 300 ft needs a modulus the density database does not supply, and several mechanical models can share an exponent, but neither gap blocks a clear test of the stated 3/2 relation.

operationalization: Estimate compressive stress from body mass and limb-bone cross-section under gravity. The claim is supported if safety factor falls with size unless bones thicken faster than isometry, and if the largest land mammals sit near a practical ceiling; it is weakened if elephants retain small-mammal safety factors or if much larger terrestrial animals have ordinary limb proportions.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D limb bones from which cross-sectional area can be measured across a body-size range

candidate_datasets.name: PHYLACINE
candidate_datasets.role: Body mass and terrestrial versus aquatic habit for living and recently extinct mammals, to locate the upper end of the size range

obstacles: Bone meshes and body-mass tables are not linked individual by individual.
Safety factors need posture and duty factor, which mass and diameter do not contain.
Food, heat, and life history can limit size even when bone stress does not.
rationale: The square-cube contrast is a definite prediction about bone allometry and maximum terrestrial mass, and both masses and scannable limb bones exist. They are not one joint dataset, mammal coverage is better than the full scope of terrestrial animals, and a thick elephant limb does not show that bone stress, rather than some other constraint, sets the ceiling. The analysis is feasible for a subset and takes more than a routine few weeks if scans must be measured and matched.

operationalization: Compare maximum mass and limb reinforcement of fully aquatic, near-neutrally buoyant mammals with terrestrial mammals. Loss of the gravitational barrier predicts much larger aquatic maxima without the same disproportionate limb bones; a hard aquatic ceiling at terrestrial masses, with the same skeletal scaling, would count against that comparative prediction.

candidate_datasets.name: PHYLACINE
candidate_datasets.role: Mammal body masses and life-habit codes separating fully aquatic from terrestrial species

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Limb and skeletal scans for comparing bone robustness of large aquatic and terrestrial mammals

obstacles: A large but finite whale is compatible both with no physical barrier and with a high barrier of another kind.
Neutral buoyancy is not measured; life-habit codes are only a coarse proxy.
rationale: Body masses of whales and land mammals, and some of their skeletons, are public, so the comparative prediction can be examined. The word indefinite has no finite confirming observation: existing size catalogs can show that aquatic maxima exceed terrestrial ones, which they do, without showing that no physical barrier remains. Buoyancy itself is assumed from habit rather than measured, so the test is a proxy for part of the claim.

operationalization: Within similar fish, fit burst speed, distance covered over a year, and time to fatigue against length. The claim predicts a steep rise of burst speed with length, little change in annual distance, and faster fatigue in smaller fish; a flat burst speed or an annual distance that scales like burst speed would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Movebank
candidate_datasets.role: Animal movement tracks, including some fishes, for distance traveled; burst speed and fatigue are not in the tracks

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Body lengths and scattered species-level swimming speeds, not size series of sprint versus endurance

obstacles: Sprint tests, fatigue curves, and annual tracks are rarely available for the same size series.
Reynolds number, temperature, and body shape change with size and can mimic the predicted exponents.
rationale: Burst speed, annual distance, and fatigue are well-defined variables, and the three-part scaling is discriminating if they are measured together within a species. What exists openly is mostly telemetry of larger individuals and uneven species-level speeds, so the joint size series has to be compiled from experimental papers. That supports a partial test, not a direct resolution of the full prediction.

operationalization: From mass and wing area, compute the mechanical power required for level flight under the fixed-proportion argument and compare its scaling with size to available muscle power. The claim is favored if required power grows near the 3.5 power of length while muscle power grows near the cube, and weakened if measured flight cost scales no faster than muscle capacity.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: Wing and body measurements for essentially all bird species, used to parameterize required flight power; muscle mass and metabolic power are not included

obstacles: External morphology does not contain muscle mass or measured flight power.
Real birds change proportions with size, so a mismatch can be read as a failed prediction or as a departure from the premise.
rationale: The exponents are explicit, and global wing morphology is public, so the geometric piece of the argument can be evaluated quickly. The work comparison itself needs flight metabolism and muscle fraction, which are scattered through wind-tunnel studies rather than present in that morphology table. Rival aerodynamic models also change the exponent, so existing open data test a restricted, model-dependent version of the claim.

operationalization: Compare required flight power with plausible muscle power at the masses and wing plans of the ostrich, moa, the heaviest flying birds, and a bird of about human mass with ordinary avian proportions. The claim is supported if moa and the man-sized bird lie beyond muscle power and the ostrich is marginal; it is weakened if birds of those masses fly with ordinary avian muscle fractions and wing shapes.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: Body size and wing measurements of extant birds, including the ostrich and the largest flying species

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil occurrences and some size data for moa, used with published mass estimates to place them on the same power comparison

obstacles: Moa mass and wing reduction are fossil estimates with wide error.
Flightlessness also evolves in birds far below any aerodynamic ceiling.
The ostrich clause is explicitly probable rather than certain.
rationale: Extant bird proportions and a biomechanical threshold make the man-sized and ostrich clauses testable in outline, and moa occurrences are in a public fossil database. The impossibility criterion is model-dependent, moa wing area is poorly known because the wings are reduced, and small flightless birds show that loss of flight is not diagnostic of having passed a size limit. The data resolve a restricted biomechanical version, not the historical claim that size is why these birds cannot fly.

operationalization: Place Carboniferous dragonfly and Jurassic pterosaur wingspans and body sizes against mechanical flight limits at modern air density, then ask whether reconstructed atmospheric density in those intervals is high enough to remove the discrepancy. Giants during a low-density interval would count against this explanation; a matching dense interval would support it.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrences and size-related records of giant insects and pterosaurs in the intervals named

candidate_datasets.name: Paleo-CO2
candidate_datasets.role: Vetted proxy reconstructions of atmospheric carbon dioxide, the compositional example Thompson offers for a denser atmosphere

obstacles: Carbon dioxide concentration is not total air density or pressure, which is what the flight calculation uses.
Oxygen, temperature, and phylogeny are alternative explanations of giant size.
Many specimens lack paired wingspan and body mass.
rationale: Fossil sizes and paleo-CO2 compilations are public, so one can ask whether the intervals of giant fliers were intervals of high CO2. That is only a proxy for the stated mechanism, because a higher proportion of carbonic acid need not raise total atmospheric density, and other environmental explanations fit the same fossils. The test can weaken this particular reconciliation; it cannot cleanly confirm denser air.

operationalization: Regress absolute jump height, or take-off velocity, on body length for animals judged similarly proportioned. A slope near zero for absolute height, together with a negative slope for height relative to body length, would support the claim; height proportional to size would refute it.
obstacles: Jump height against size, from small jumpers to large mammals, is scattered through papers rather than held in one public dataset.
Elastic tendons and crouched postures violate the similar-construction premise and change the expected scaling.
rationale: Absolute versus relative jump height is a sharp, measurable contrast, so operationalizability and discriminating power are high. The obstacle is the data: published jump performances would have to be compiled, they do not span the flea-to-horse range under a common protocol, and similar construction is a judgment rather than a column in a table. Existing numbers can test a mammal subset after months of harmonization, which is only a partial resolution.

operationalization: Fit log speed on log length separately for swimming, flight, and walking among animals of similar construction. An exponent near one-half in each case would support the claim; exponents near zero or one would favor the obvious rivals.

candidate_datasets.name: Movebank
candidate_datasets.role: Tracked movement speeds that can be paired with body size for some walking, flying, and swimming animals

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Body lengths and species-level swimming speeds for the swimming case of the square-root relation

obstacles: Tracked speeds are mostly routine movement, not minimum flight speed, sprint speed, or pendulum walking speed.
Cross-species samples mix mechanical design with the size effect the claim sets aside.
rationale: The shared square-root prediction is precise and could be distinguished from other exponents with size-matched speeds. Open tracking and fisheries databases contain speeds and lengths, but not the three theoretical speeds the derivations name, and similar construction is hard to enforce. A careful subset analysis is feasible; it would not settle all three modes together.

operationalization: The doubled-gravity fauna is not in any dataset. A proxy is whether limb proportions become shorter and more heavily built as body weight, and thus skeletal load, increases. That pattern would support the scaling the counterfactual extrapolates; it would not show what animals would be like under twice or half Earth's gravity.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Limb bones for measuring relative length and robustness against body size, as a proxy for load

candidate_datasets.name: PHYLACINE
candidate_datasets.role: Terrestrial mammal body masses to place limb proportions on a size axis

obstacles: The claim is a counterfactual about a different gravitational constant.
Short legs have many ecological causes besides skeletal load.
rationale: No existing dataset records terrestrial animals that evolved under doubled or halved gravity, so the literal prediction cannot be confirmed or refuted. Limb allometry against mass is a public proxy for the idea that gravitational load conditions form, and it is only a proxy: a short-legged large mammal is compatible with several selective stories. Discriminating power stays low for that reason.

operationalization: Measure surface area and mass for gut lining and cerebral cortex across body sizes. Surface per mass staying roughly constant, with folding or villi increasing with size, would support the claim; a smooth surface scaling as volume to the two-thirds would refute it for that organ.

candidate_datasets.name: Allen Brain Atlas
candidate_datasets.role: Quantified cortical surface for human and mouse brains, a narrow taxonomic slice of the folding comparison

candidate_datasets.name: Comparative Mammalian Brain Collections
candidate_datasets.role: Section images of many mammal brains from which folding can be scored; surface area is not a delivered measurement

obstacles: Gut and brain surface areas are scattered by species and by measurement method.
Brain-image archives are dominated by a few model species rather than a body-size series.
rationale: An invariant surface-to-mass ratio is a clear alternative to geometric scaling of a smooth surface, and brain images plus a few atlases make a start on cortex. They do not contain a cross-species surface-and-mass table, and intestinal villi and the shark spiral valve are even less centralized. The tendency throughout morphology can be probed for one or two organs only.

operationalization: Score sphericity, or departure from a constant-mean-curvature shape, against body or cell size, and compare gravitational stress with a surface-stress estimate. Small organisms clustering on those simple shapes, and large animals' external forms not doing so, would support the descriptive half; assigning the cause to surface tension rather than a wall or cytoskeleton requires the force comparison.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Cell and small-organism images for measuring how close outlines are to spheres and other simple shapes

candidate_datasets.name: Cell Image Library
candidate_datasets.role: Additional cell and protist images across a limited size range

obstacles: Walls, internal pressure, and cortical tension produce spherical outlines without classical surface tension.
Image collections over-represent model cells rather than a size gradient of whole organisms.
rationale: Sphericity versus size is measurable on existing images, and large-animal external form is obviously not a surface-tension minimum, so part of the contrast can be checked. The causal attribution is a reinterpretation, and spheres have several mechanical explanations, so shape catalogs do not cleanly favor surface tension over those rivals. Coverage of the smallest organisms is patchy.

operationalization: For large organisms, test whether the change in external shape equals the integral of directional growth rates. For cells and minute organisms, test whether shape is uncorrelated with those rates once surface or intermolecular forces are accounted for. A large organism whose form changed mainly by migration or cell death without anisotropic growth would count against the first clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Time-lapse and developmental images from which cell shape and, in some studies, local growth can be measured

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Ontogenetic specimen series for a few larger taxa, giving shape but not growth rates directly

obstacles: Directional growth rates and shape are seldom in the same public file.
Anisotropic growth can be a redescription of shape change, which weakens the contrast with rivals.
rationale: The large-versus-minute contrast is testable in principle with growth maps, and some public images and ontogenetic scans exist. They do not jointly cover rates and form across the two regimes, and for multicellular growth the rate-ratio account is close to a kinematic identity. Discriminating it from patterning, migration, and mechanical deformation needs data that are still mostly in individual studies.

operationalization: Measure surface and volume of a cell before and after division, including cleaving eggs. An increase of surface at constant volume confirms the geometric clause. The further claim, that division restores a characteristic surface-to-mass ratio and an energy balance, requires that division be better predicted by departure of that ratio than by genome content or a timer.

candidate_datasets.name: BioNumbers
candidate_datasets.role: Cell volumes, surface-related sizes, and division sizes for model cells and early embryos

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Imaging studies of dividing cells from which mother and daughter surface and volume can be segmented

obstacles: A surface increase at cleavage, with mass held constant, is nearly guaranteed by geometry.
Surface and volume do not identify an energetic purpose of division.
rationale: Mother-daughter sizes are widely measured, so the geometric effect of cleavage is immediately checkable and will generally hold. That success does not discriminate the claim that division happens in order to restore surface energy, because other division triggers produce the same surface increase. The energetic half remains only partly testable with existing size data.

operationalization: For each cell type, compare the spread of cell size with the spread of body size across dwarf and giant individuals or related species, and partition the body-size difference into cell size versus cell number. The claim is confirmed if cell size stays in a narrow band and cell number accounts for body size; it is refuted if homologous cells scale up with the body.

candidate_datasets.name: BioNumbers
candidate_datasets.role: Published cell sizes and counts for comparing within-type variation with body size

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Microscopy datasets from which cell size distributions can be measured in model tissues

obstacles: Public sizes are dense for a few tissues and model species, not for the Crepidula and urchin cases named.
Polyploid and hypertrophic tissues are real exceptions and have to be separated by cell class.
rationale: Cell size versus cell number is a clean partition, and both quantities are routine to analyse once tabulated. Existing compilations and images cover enough mammalian and model tissues for a strong subset test, but not the claim's full scope of every cell kind across dwarf and giant animals. Building that table is a months-scale harmonization, so the claim is partly resolvable now.

operationalization: Compare neuronal soma size and the number of cells per ganglion across species that differ widely in body size. A narrow soma-size range, with fewer cells in smaller species, would support the claim; soma size scaling with body size, or no trend in cell number, would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: NeuroMorpho.Org
candidate_datasets.role: Digitally reconstructed neurons from many species, with soma and arbor measurements that can be compared across body sizes

obstacles: Reconstructions over-represent mammalian cortex rather than whole ganglia of small invertebrates.
Soma size in a reconstruction archive is not a random sample of ganglion cells, and complete cell counts are a thinner subset.
rationale: Soma size and cell number are the variables the claim names, and a large open archive of neuronal morphologies spans many species, including some very large and very small animals. That archive is a biased sample of neuron classes, not a survey of ganglia, so the law as stated for animals in general can be tested only on a restricted and non-random subset. The analysis itself is standard once the subset is defined.

operationalization: Compare the lower tail of free-living cell diameter with the volume of a minimal genome plus ribosomes. The claim is supported if that tail sits near the packing floor corresponding to tens of thousands of proteins; it is weakened if diverse free-living organisms are far smaller than that floor allows.

candidate_datasets.name: BacDive
candidate_datasets.role: Strain-level bacterial cell dimensions for the observed lower end of organism size

candidate_datasets.name: BioNumbers
candidate_datasets.role: Ribosome, protein, and genome-related sizes used to compute a molecular packing floor

obstacles: Culture collections miss many of the smallest uncultured cells.
Where an object stops being an organism and becomes a virus is a definitional boundary at the lower limit.
rationale: Cell dimensions and the sizes of the molecular parts that fill them are both in public databases, so the 1917 comparison of a minute micrococcus with molecular magnitudes can be rerun directly. The further claim that organisms cannot be much smaller is only partly closed by catalogs of known cells, and the organism boundary matters. The data can confirm that the known minimum is near a packing limit, without exhausting undiscovered smaller forms.

operationalization: Compare external shape change with the ratios of extension along principal directions, excluding the minute organisms the claim sets aside. The informative contrast is with form change produced by rearrangement, cell death, or buckling without local growth differences; pure redescription of every shape change as a growth-rate ratio would not decide the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Growth series of larger organisms for measuring directional change in external form

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Cellular and developmental imaging for the minute-organism cases excluded from the growth-ratio account

obstacles: Growth-rate ratios are often a redescription of the shape change they are asked to explain.
Paired growth and shape series exist for a minority of organisms.
rationale: Directional growth and external form can be measured on existing growth series for some animals and plants. Because any smooth change of outline can be written as anisotropic growth, most datasets are compatible with the claim and with rivals that emphasize migration or mechanics. Only studies that separate local growth from those other contributions are discriminating, and they are a subset that still has to be assembled.

operationalization: Track ratios of growth along different axes through time. Constant ratios should coincide with increase in bulk at stable shape, and a change in the ratios with a persistent change of form. The seasonal clause is tested by whether isometric intervals usually end within about one growing season.

candidate_datasets.name: ICES DATRAS
candidate_datasets.role: Repeated length and weight measurements that proxy body form across seasons in fishes

candidate_datasets.name: Add-my-Pet
candidate_datasets.role: Referenced age-length and age-weight series for many animals, used to see how long form stays stable

obstacles: Length and weight are a single-number proxy for multi-axis form.
Seasonal feeding and spawning can mimic a change in the growth-rate ratio.
rationale: The link between a constant ratio and stable form is a standard morphometric test, and multi-age size series exist for many animals. Most of those series do not resolve several body axes, so they proxy the claim rather than measure the ratios named in it, and a season is hard to score outside well-sampled fishes. The pattern can be tested on a restricted scope.

operationalization: Map local expansion rate across the blastoderm and compare it with the sites of neural and amniotic folds. Folds sitting where an initially even sheet grows unequally would support the claim; folds formed by active bending where growth is uniform would count against growth inequality as the essential cause.

candidate_datasets.name: Image Data Resource
candidate_datasets.role: Developmental imaging studies that include vertebrate embryos, from which local deformation can sometimes be measured

obstacles: Strain and proliferation maps are in individual studies, not in a general embryo archive.
Contractile folding can coincide with growth differences, so the two causes are hard to separate.
rationale: Unequal growth versus active bending is a genuine contrast, and chick and mouse embryos have been imaged in ways that can locate folds relative to expansion. Those maps are not a single open resource matched to neural and amniotic folds, and the two mechanisms co-occur. A small team could reanalyse a few published datasets, which tests the chick-centered case rather than vertebrate embryos in general.

operationalization: Measure size and shape disparity among related species at successive ages, including fetal stages. Disparity small in the young and increasing toward the adult would support the claim; disparity already large at the earliest comparable stages would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Ontogenetic specimen series for comparing juvenile and adult disparity in size and shape

obstacles: Fetal and juvenile series are taxonomically sparse next to adult specimens.
Museum sampling favors adults, which can exaggerate apparent late divergence.
rationale: Age-related disparity is a standard morphometric question, and some public ontogenetic series bear on it. The claim covers related individuals and species, especially mammals traced through fetal stages, and fetal series of that breadth are not in one open collection. Existing scans can test a biased subset, with a real risk that preservation, not biology, produces the gradual pattern.

operationalization: Plot stature velocity against age from birth to adult height. The claim is confirmed by high infantile velocity, a lower and nearly steady childhood velocity, a distinct acceleration in the early teens, and a decline to zero at adult height. A single smooth peak, or no adolescent acceleration, would refute that phasing.

candidate_datasets.name: WHO Child Growth Standards
candidate_datasets.role: Age-specific stature from birth through childhood, from which velocity phases can be estimated

candidate_datasets.name: NHANES
candidate_datasets.role: Open measured stature by age from infancy through adulthood for the adolescent acceleration and the final arrest

obstacles: Populations differ in the age of the adolescent peak, so one universal calendar age is too strict.
The original description was drawn largely from boys.
rationale: National examinations and international growth standards record stature by age in very large samples, and velocity is obtained from them by ordinary smoothing. The four-phase pattern is specific enough to fail if the adolescent quickening is absent. Population differences in timing are a real caveat, but they do not prevent a direct confirmation or refutation of the stated sequence.

operationalization: Compare stature in the same adults from early adulthood to before 50, around 60, and in advanced old age. A loss beginning well before 50 and becoming marked by 60 would support the claim; stable height until advanced old age would refute the stated timing.

candidate_datasets.name: NHANES
candidate_datasets.role: Cross-sectional measured height by adult age, an open but confounded proxy for individual shrinkage

obstacles: Cross-sectional height-by-age mixes shrinkage with the secular increase in peak height.
Longitudinal series that separate those effects are less directly downloadable than NHANES.
rationale: The age thresholds are explicit, and open survey data give mean height by year of age for tens of thousands of adults. Because later-born cohorts are taller, older people being shorter does not by itself show loss of stature in the individual, which is what the claim asserts. Longitudinal studies exist and could resolve that, but the openly analysed cross-section remains a partial and confounded test.

operationalization: Fit log weight on log height through childhood and adolescence, and compare the weight curve with the cube of the stature curve. A slope near 3, and an alignment of the two curves after that cubic transformation, would support the claim; a slope far from 3, or a residual shape difference that the cube does not remove, would count against the claim that the cube is the main reason the curves differ.

candidate_datasets.name: NHANES
candidate_datasets.role: Paired measured height and weight across growing ages

candidate_datasets.name: WHO Child Growth Standards
candidate_datasets.role: Reference height and weight curves for the same cubic comparison in early growth

obstacles: Changing proportions and body composition move the exponent off 3, which the claim already allows as not the whole explanation.
rationale: Paired height and weight through human growth are among the most completely published biological measurements, and the cube-law regression is immediate. The claim is already hedged as a tendency and as the main rather than the only reason the weight curve differs from the stature curve, and those hedges can be scored by how much of the curve difference the cubic term removes. That is a direct test with existing open data.

operationalization: Estimate stature-velocity curves separately for girls and boys. The claim is confirmed if the curves share the same sequence of phases, with the female adolescent acceleration starting and ending earlier and amplitude allowed to differ. Identical timing, or a different sequence of phases, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: WHO Child Growth Standards
candidate_datasets.role: Sex-specific stature references from which childhood and adolescent velocities can be compared

candidate_datasets.name: NHANES
candidate_datasets.role: Sex-specific measured stature by age through the adolescent acceleration

obstacles: The size of the age gap is population-dependent, so the phase shift should be tested within populations.
rationale: Sex-specific growth references are public, large, and already tabulated by age. Estimating the two velocity curves and the lag of the male acceleration is a standard calculation that would clearly fail if the female spurt were not earlier or if the phase sequence differed. Population variation in the size of the lag does not remove that contrast.

operationalization: From age-length or age-weight series, locate the age of maximum growth velocity and the later decline toward cessation, in both long-lived and short-lived species. An early maximum followed by slowdown would support the shared sequence; a maximum at the start of growth, or no slowdown, in a large clade would limit the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Add-my-Pet
candidate_datasets.role: Referenced growth trajectories and fitted life-cycle parameters across animal phyla

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Age and growth parameters for fishes, to be used with raw length-at-age where the fitted curve does not hide an early lag

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge
candidate_datasets.role: Longevity records used to separate long-lived from short-lived species in the comparison

obstacles: Von Bertalanffy fits force the maximum growth rate to the origin and can hide an early slow start.
Invertebrates are much less completely measured than mammals and commercial fishes.
rationale: A common sequence of a slow start, an early peak, and a slowdown is visible in compiled growth trajectories for many vertebrates, and longevity databases classify the life-span contrast the claim draws. The universal quantifier over all animals is not matched by the taxonomic coverage, and the most common fisheries growth model assumes away the early lag. The phases can be recovered for a biased but substantial subset if raw series are used instead of those fits.

operationalization: Using raw length-at-age for fishes, test whether growth increments decline toward zero without a sharp stop, rather than ceasing at a characteristic adult length. Continued slow growth at old ages would support an asymptote; a long terminal period of literally zero growth would count against it. Fitted asymptotic parameters should not be the evidence, because many were estimated by assuming that form.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Growth studies and length-at-age sources for many fishes; published asymptotic parameters are a circular summary and raw ages are the usable part

candidate_datasets.name: ICES DATRAS
candidate_datasets.role: Survey length and age data for testing whether increments keep declining at large size

obstacles: Published von Bertalanffy parameters assume an asymptote and cannot be used as the test.
Survey gear under-samples the oldest fish, and some species do stop growing.
rationale: The asymptotic pattern is a specific alternative to determinate cessation, and raw length-at-age for many fishes is publicly downloadable from survey and life-history databases. A small team can estimate increments at old ages without assuming the curve the claim asserts. Gear bias and genuine exceptions among ectotherms limit how far the result generalizes, but they do not prevent a direct test of the fish case on which the claim centers.

operationalization: Decompose adult size into a rate parameter and a duration for human, rabbit, and guinea pig, and then across mammals more generally. The named contrasts predict a higher rate for the rabbit than the guinea pig and a longer duration for the human than the rabbit. A model that uses only rate or only duration should fail if both factors matter.

candidate_datasets.name: Add-my-Pet
candidate_datasets.role: Growth data and life-cycle parameters for human, rabbit, guinea pig, and many other mammals

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge
candidate_datasets.role: Adult body mass and longevity as coarse correlates of size and growth duration

candidate_datasets.name: WHO Child Growth Standards
candidate_datasets.role: Human postnatal growth rate and the long duration of human growth

obstacles: Energy-budget parameters already impose a rate-duration decomposition, so they are not a fully independent test.
Nutrition in the classical laboratory comparisons is not standardized across species.
rationale: Rate and duration are separable on existing growth curves, and the three named species are represented in public life-history compilations and human growth standards. That is enough to check the rabbit-guinea pig and human-rabbit contrasts. Extending the result to mammals in general is limited by uneven raw curves, and model-based parameters partly build in the decomposition they are asked to test, so the general claim is only partly resolved.

operationalization: Estimate human fetal length velocity by gestational age. A maximum near the fifth month, with velocity rising before it and falling after, would support the claim. A maximum far from that month, or no inflection, would refute it. Femur length or crown-rump length may stand in for crown-heel length if the two are shown to share the same velocity peak.

candidate_datasets.name: INTERGROWTH-21st
candidate_datasets.role: International fetal biometry by gestational age, used to locate the velocity maximum of prenatal linear growth

obstacles: Modern standards usually record femur length or crown-rump length rather than the crown-heel length of the older curves.
Dating error and cross-sectional sampling can shift the apparent month of the inflection.
rationale: Fetal size by week of gestation is tabulated in a large public standard, and locating a velocity maximum is a direct calculation. The fifth-month inflection is specific enough to fail if the peak lies elsewhere. The remaining weakness is that the measured length is often a skeletal segment rather than whole-body length, so the test is exact only if that proxy tracks the length Thompson plotted. That is a limited measurement issue, not a missing dataset.

operationalization: Compute the coefficient of variation of stature and of weight by age, and the mean growth velocity at the same ages. The claim predicts that the coefficient falls as velocity falls through childhood and rises again with the adolescent acceleration. A flat coefficient through the adolescent spurt would refute that association.

candidate_datasets.name: NHANES
candidate_datasets.role: Individual stature and weight by age, so both the age-specific coefficient of variation and the mean velocity can be estimated

candidate_datasets.name: WHO Child Growth Standards
candidate_datasets.role: Published percentiles by age, an alternative estimate of spread against growth rate in childhood

obstacles: Adolescent variance rises partly because children enter the spurt at different ages, which is related to but not identical with a higher growth rate.
Weight variation is also affected by body composition.
rationale: Both the spread of stature and weight and the mean rate of growth are estimable from the same open age-specific surveys, and the predicted rise and fall of variability is a definite pattern. Tempo variation at adolescence is a serious confound for the interpretation that variability is a function of the rate itself, but it is measurable in the same data and does not make every outcome compatible with the claim. The association can be confirmed or refuted with a standard analysis.

operationalization: Test for a change in the slope of growth rate at birth and at puberty in humans, and at metamorphosis in insects, amphibians, and other transforming animals. Marked slope changes at those epochs, strongest where metamorphosis is regular, would support the claim; smooth velocity through them would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: NHANES
candidate_datasets.role: Human stature velocity around puberty; birth is only the left edge of the postnatal series

candidate_datasets.name: Add-my-Pet
candidate_datasets.role: Life-cycle trajectories for species with metamorphosis, including some amphibians and insects

obstacles: Human birth and puberty effects are modest and easy to confuse with a change of environment or measurement.
Metamorphic growth series are not gathered as a single designed dataset.
rationale: Interruptions at named physiological epochs can be looked for in human growth surveys and in compiled animal life cycles. The human adolescent case is well powered; birth and, especially, metamorphosis depend on scattered series, and a slope change at an epoch that coincides with a change of habitat is only partly discriminating. The general claim is therefore testable in pieces.

operationalization: Compare live mass just before and just after metamorphosis in eels, insects such as the silkworm, and amphibian tadpoles. A net loss would support the claim for that species; a well-measured metamorphic group that does not lose mass would weaken the suggestion that the loss always occurs.

candidate_datasets.name: Add-my-Pet
candidate_datasets.role: Referenced weights through the life cycle for some metamorphic species; coverage of the loss itself is uneven

obstacles: Weight series through metamorphosis are scattered across experimental papers.
Loss of water or gut contents can be recorded as loss of bulk without loss of tissue.
rationale: A loss of mass at metamorphosis is a simple before-after contrast, and published series for the eel, silkworm, and frog exist to be compiled. There is no open dataset designed for that contrast across metamorphic animals, so the universal suggestion cannot be closed, and water loss confounds tissue loss. The named cases are partly resolvable; the claim in full is not.

operationalization: Plot brain, heart, and liver mass as fractions of body mass from birth to adult ages. For the human brain, the claim predicts a fall from about one-eighth of body weight at birth to about one-fiftieth at age 25. A ratio that stays constant over that span would refute the claim; the same test applied to heart, liver, lion, and dogfish needs their own series.

candidate_datasets.name: OpenNeuro
candidate_datasets.role: Public MRI volumes across ages for estimating human brain size; body mass is often stored separately

candidate_datasets.name: NHANES
candidate_datasets.role: Body mass by age, the denominator of the organ-to-body ratio when brain volume comes from another archive

obstacles: MRI volume and autopsy weight are not the same quantity, and body mass is often not in the imaging file.
The lion and dogfish series are not in these human-centered archives.
rationale: A constant organ-to-body ratio is a sharp null, and human brain volume plus body mass by age are each publicly available, though usually not in the same file. Joining them can test the human brain fractions, which are the quantitative core of the claim. Heart, liver, and the non-human examples remain scattered, so the claim throughout life and across the vertebrates cited is only partly covered.

operationalization: For plaice, compute k = W/L^3 by length bin and compare the length of the maximum with the length at which maturity begins. A rise to a maximum and a later slow decline, with that maximum near 30 cm and near the maturity ogive, would support the claim. A flat k, or a maximum far from maturity, would refute the stated pattern.

candidate_datasets.name: ICES DATRAS
candidate_datasets.role: Individual plaice length, weight, and maturity stage from surveys that cover the North Sea stocks

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Length-weight parameters and life-history notes for plaice as a cross-check on the survey calculation

obstacles: Seasonal condition and gear selectivity can shift the apparent maximum.
The 30 cm figure belongs to the stocks Thompson knew; other plaice stocks may mature at another length.
rationale: Individual length, weight, and maturity for plaice are in a long-running open trawl-survey database, so k against length and the maturity comparison are routine. The predicted hump is specific enough to fail. Stock differences and season can move the peak, and those factors can be stratified in the same data rather than left as an uncontrolled confound. The extension to other fishes is extra; the plaice claim itself is resolvable now.

operationalization: At fixed length, test whether plaice weight falls from about November to March or April and recovers from May or June to November, and whether that cycle is confined to mature fish and matched by gonad loss. The claim that spawning wholly explains the cycle is refuted by the same cycle in immature fish, or by a large residual cycle after gonad mass is removed.

candidate_datasets.name: ICES DATRAS
candidate_datasets.role: Seasonal plaice length, weight, and maturity stage, including age-length keys by sex and maturity

obstacles: Not every haul records individual weight and maturity together.
Seasonal feeding can change somatic condition even when the gonad cycle is the larger term.
rationale: The months, the fixed-length comparison, and the spawning mechanism are all specified, and the relevant survey records are public. Immature fish are the discriminating control for the word wholly. Incomplete maturity staging and a feeding residual are real limits, but they are analysable in the same tables and do not leave the claim untestable.

operationalization: Estimate a specific growth rate for the whole body and for separate organs, then ask how much adult shape difference those local rate differences produce. The claim is favored if small, persistent rate differences account for a large share of between-species form; it is hard to refute, because no share is named as too small.

candidate_datasets.name: Add-my-Pet
candidate_datasets.role: Whole-organism growth rates across species; organ-specific rates are not the main content

candidate_datasets.name: BioNumbers
candidate_datasets.role: Scattered organ and body sizes at different stages, from which crude local growth can sometimes be inferred

obstacles: Organ-specific growth rates are published piecemeal.
A very large part of specific morphology does not state how large a part would fail the claim.
rationale: Organ growth curves exist in the literature and can show that local rates differ, which is the easier half of the claim. Public compilations are still mostly whole-body, and the assertion that a large part of species-specific form depends on those local rates has no sharp failure threshold. Sensitivity of shape to small rate changes is partly a mathematical property of exponential growth, so it does not by itself discriminate this account from rivals. The test stays partial.

operationalization: From growth rate versus temperature, estimate the optimum for common temperate plants and for melon and maize. A shared temperate optimum near 26°C, and a higher optimum for melon and maize, would support the claim. A wide scatter of temperate optima, or no elevation for the warm-climate species, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: Plant traits including some growth measurements; full temperature-response curves are mostly still in the agronomic papers TRY points toward

obstacles: Optimum curves are scattered by species, organ (root versus shoot), and protocol.
Temperate crops are heavily over-represented relative to the common wild flora.
rationale: An optimum temperature is a standard parameter of a growth-response curve, and the numerical contrast between about 26°C and a higher warm-climate optimum is discriminating. The curves themselves are spread through experimental papers rather than collected as one open file, and what is well measured is a subset of crops, not the common plants of temperate climates. Compiling that subset is feasible and would resolve only part of the stated scope.

operationalization: Below the optimum, compute the factor by which growth rate changes per 10°C. A factor of about 2 to 3, the same order as ordinary chemical reactions, would support the claim. A factor near 1 across the normal range, or systematically an order of magnitude larger, would refute the stated similarity. Intervals above the optimum are outside the qualified claim.

candidate_datasets.name: BioNumbers
candidate_datasets.role: Published Q10 and rate values for growth and related physiological processes

candidate_datasets.name: Add-my-Pet
candidate_datasets.role: Temperature-correction parameters fitted to growth and development for many animals

obstacles: The coefficient itself falls as the temperature interval rises, so the test range has to be declared.
Fitted temperature parameters are not the same object as a raw rate ratio, and tabulated Q10 values are a sparse sample.
rationale: A Q10 between about 2 and 3 is a numerical criterion, and both raw rates and fitted temperature coefficients exist for many species. They are not one openly complete table for plants and animals inside normal limits, and the coefficient's dependence on the chosen interval is a built-in ambiguity the claim already flags. A compiled subset can test the order of magnitude; it does not cover the full scope in a single standard analysis.

operationalization: Separate a short-term accelerating effect of temperature from a cumulative damaging effect, for example by comparing brief exposures above a putative optimum with long exposures. The claim predicts that an optimum curve appears only when both effects act. An instantaneous equilibrium optimum, with no extra damage from duration, would count against that two-process account.

candidate_datasets.name: BioNumbers
candidate_datasets.role: Temperature coefficients and rates that document optima, without a direct measure of cumulative damage

candidate_datasets.name: Add-my-Pet
candidate_datasets.role: Temperature corrections of growth, mostly a single accelerating function rather than a damage time course

obstacles: Cumulative damage or fatigue is not a column beside growth rate.
Protein denaturation and other single mechanisms also produce an optimum curve.
rationale: Acute versus chronic thermal performance can in principle separate cumulative damage from an instantaneous optimum, and growth-versus-temperature data exist to support pieces of that contrast. Public compilations store a rate or a single temperature coefficient, not the time course of damage, and several molecular rivals fit the same optimum curve. The mechanistic claim is only partly operational and only partly supplied with data.
